description: City Council voted unanimously to enact a 6-month moratorium on data centers requiring >20 MW. Exempts DC Blox and Nebius AI Factory.
City Council passed a one-year moratorium on data centers in early June 2026.
City Council approved a 12-month moratorium (extendable by six months) on data centers on June 22, 2026.
City Council unanimously imposed a 12-month moratorium on June 22, 2026 and referred a prohibition zoning amendment to the Planning Commission.
City Council unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on data centers on June 16, 2026.

City Council adopted Resolution No. 26-R-97 on August 18, 2026, a 12-month moratorium (effective immediately, extendable or shortenable) on the permitting, development and licensing of data centers within its regulatory jurisdiction. Directs the Planning Commission to study siting, lot sizes, electrical demand, water use, stormwater, backup generators and noise, and report within six months.

City Council unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on data centers on August 18, 2026, after residents voiced concerns over a proposed 437-acre data center project near Cheshire Drive. Officials will review zoning and community impact conditions during the pause.

The town adopted a six-month data center moratorium in early September 2026 as a proactive measure despite no developer interest, with monthly informational sessions planned on energy, water and environmental concerns.

City Council unanimously approved an ordinance classifying data centers and battery storage as conditional uses in manufacturing and warehouse zones, requiring Board of Zoning Adjustment review and public hearings; the city's six-month moratorium remains in effect through December 15, 2026.

Foley approved a 6-month moratorium on September 14, 2026 halting data center, cryptocurrency-mining and server-farm applications while the city updates ordinances covering water, air pollution and noise.
Assembly adopted preemptive data center regulations: requires conditional use permits, 200-foot setbacks, visual screening, fire suppression, and noise mitigation for facilities using 20+ MW.
Ongoing restrictions limiting data centers to planned developments only. Concerns over noise and limited job creation.
City advancing code amendment to regulate large-scale data centers; public meetings since Feb 2026

City approved its first large-scale data center rules 6-1. Facilities over 25,000 sq ft or 20 MW must maintain a half-mile residential buffer, cap height at 50 feet, disclose energy sources, stay within potable water limits, and obtain mayor and council approval.

Board of Supervisors narrowly approved a 120-day moratorium on September 22, 2026 on new data center projects in unincorporated areas — pausing permits and project advancement while the county drafts code requirements that could include closed-loop cooling, noise reduction and design standards, with draft code text expected by December. On October 28, 2026 the county's Planning and Zoning Commission voted 8-1 to advance ordinance amendments requiring a Type 3 conditional use permit for data centers in the CI-2 heavy industrial zone (about 2% of county land), conditioned on staff addressing monitoring, noise, water limits and a narrower data center definition; a revised proposal goes to the Board of Supervisors in early December.

The town is moving to ban data centers of 20 MW or more (reported the week of October 26, 2026); only ancillary facilities such as server rooms would be allowed, each requiring a conditional use permit.

A proposed ordinance would ban open-loop evaporative cooling, require a 650-foot residential setback and bar the use of potable water for cooling. The council postponed action the week of October 26, 2026, with revised rules due December 15.

Quorum Court voted down a proposed 12-month moratorium on data center construction 10-3 (one justice voting "present") on July 28, 2026. Critics objected that a carve-out exempting the AVAIO Digital Wrightsville project amounted to a "free pass"; a separate amendment to close the carve-out also failed.
Quorum court unanimously enacted a five-year moratorium on data centers running through 2031, citing existing strain on local water supply, despite no specific project being proposed.
Quorum court voted 8-0 for a three-year moratorium on data centers, effective immediately, with no known project in development. The second-longest pause in Arkansas.
County adopted a one-year moratorium on data centers in June 2026.
Quorum court unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on data centers in June 2026.
City adopted a six-month moratorium on data centers in July 2026.

The city board rejected a six-month moratorium on large data centers on a 4-4 tie on October 20, 2026 — the second failed attempt after an 18-month proposal failed in August — as Google's $1B data center project looms.

The Quorum Court passed the ordinance regulating 'high-density digital infrastructure' 11-4 on September 22, 2026 — classifying large data centers as heavy industrial uses requiring conditional use permits and addressing electrical demand, water/wastewater capacity, noise, roads, drainage, emergency response and decommissioning, with no carve-out for AVAIO Digital's planned $6 billion Wrightsville project. County Judge Barry Hyde vetoed the ordinance on September 24, calling it a legal and financial risk; an override requires 9 of 15 votes, with a vote possible October 27.

City Council approved an ordinance on September 15, 2026 restricting data center campuses to I-3 heavy industrial zones under conditional use permits that require developers to demonstrate utility capacity.

City Council unanimously adopted 45-day moratorium on data center applications, later extended through January 2027. Council voted to place a permanent citywide data center ban on the June 2026 ballot.

After a Superior Court judge struck down the county's earlier data center moratorium in September 2026 for insufficient findings, the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously on October 6, 2026 to reinstate a temporary emergency moratorium, calling data centers a 'current and immediate threat' to the valley's water supply; two supervisors are pressing for a special election on data center limits.
City Council voted unanimously to extend its temporary moratorium on new data center projects, giving staff more time to evaluate community impacts.

Board of Supervisors voted 5-0 on September 22, 2026 to extend the county's data center moratorium in unincorporated areas by 10 months while staff complete a regulatory review and draft permanent zoning rules; options under evaluation include conditional use permits, zoning requirements, or an outright ban. Original 45-day moratorium was adopted August 19, 2026. On September 30, 2026 the Board of Supervisors additionally adopted a formal position opposing data center development in the county on a 3-2 vote.
City Council passed a permanent ban on data centers within city limits on August 25, 2026, making Coachella the third Riverside County city to ban them after Perris and Desert Hot Springs.
City issued a policy statement opposing data centers without meaningful local review; current zoning prohibits data centers and no change is planned.

City Council voted on September 28, 2026 (with the required four-fifths majority) to extend the city's data center moratorium through August 25, 2028 — a 22-month extension of the 45-day urgency ordinance originally adopted August 26, 2026 — while the city studies water, energy and infrastructure impacts and writes permanent zoning rules.

Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 on October 6, 2026 to extend the September 1 urgency moratorium (originally set to expire October 16) through August 21, 2028, adding an exemption for facilities drawing under 3 MW.

City Council unanimously approved a 45-day urgency moratorium on AI data centers and expansions in late August 2026, framed as a public health and safety measure; staff findings are due October 10, with extensions of up to a year possible. No applications are currently pending.

City Council voted 7-0 on September 3, 2026 to direct staff to draft a Development Code text amendment banning data centers citywide for 10 years, applying to current and future city land; Mayor Jerry Dyer co-sponsored the measure. Staff estimate the amendment could take several months to a year to return for adoption.

locality: City and County of San Francisco
description: The Board of Supervisors unanimously passed Supervisor Shamann Walton's interim moratorium on new data centers on October 13, 2026, and Mayor Daniel Lurie signed it on October 16, 2026. The 45-day citywide pause on new data center approvals can be extended to roughly 22 months while planning staff study energy, water, air quality, land use and community impacts; a hearing is due by November. Two projects are halted: a NOVVA site in Bayview and a 49.5 MW Dogpatch building.
The Board of Supervisors rejected a proposed requirement that AI data center projects receive voter approval; sponsor Supervisor Cummings may pursue a ballot petition instead.

City Council voted 3-0 on September 16, 2026 to ban data centers via a zoning code amendment, becoming the third California city to do so; the ordinance formalizes that data centers are not a permitted use following the city's June moratorium process.

City Council voted unanimously on October 6, 2026 to enact a 45-day moratorium on new data center development, effective immediately and extendable by another 45 days, while staff study energy, water, public health and environmental impacts.

City Council adopted Urgency Ordinance No. 13-26 N.S. on September 15, 2026 — a 45-day moratorium on issuing or approving permits and land-use entitlements for new data centers, expiring October 30, 2026. A public hearing on October 20, 2026 will consider extending it by 22 months and 15 days while the city studies impacts.

The city council extended Gilroy's data center moratorium by 10 months and 15 days on October 19, 2026; the pause does not affect the $2B AWS facility already under construction but covers any future application, including a possible second Amazon facility.
Supervisors voted on October 20, 2026 to begin evaluating zoning limits on data centers in unincorporated areas; a countywide ban was dropped from the original proposal.
The city council extended Hawthorne's moratorium on new and expanded data centers through September 2027 on October 13, 2026, while officials weigh permanent rules.

Mayor Todd Gloria signed Executive Order 2026-2 on October 22, 2026 directing a temporary moratorium on new data center development and creating a Data Center Stakeholder Working Group, with department recommendations due within 180 days. The City Council unanimously ratified the 45-day moratorium on data center permitting, approval and development on October 27, 2026. The action followed reports that Manchester Financial Group was weighing a 400 MW data center at the Navy's NAVWAR site, federal land over which the city has limited authority.

City Council unanimously adopted a 45-day moratorium on new data center development at a special meeting in late October 2026, effective immediately. The pause targets phases two and three of the AVAIO data center project at the former Delta View Golf Course; phase one, approved in 2024, is unaffected. Residents pressed for a longer two-year halt, and the council can consider extending the pause before it expires.
Voters approved a citywide data center ban with ~83% support on November 3, 2026 — one of five full bans passed nationally that day and the first voter-enacted citywide data center ban in California.
City Council unanimously (9-0) approved Ordinance 2313 on July 7, 2026, an 18-month moratorium through December 2027 on new data centers using 10 MW or more.

City Council voted unanimously on May 18, 2026 to enact a one-year moratorium on new data center zoning permits and site development plans. Exempts already-permitted work (CoreSite's DE3 grandfathered; two additional planned buildings halted) and telecom-focused facilities. Prompted by Stage 1 drought and Denver Water's call for 20% water reduction; city forming a task force.
Moratorium on new data center permits in unincorporated areas, extended to August 25, 2026. County developing specific land-use regulations for data centers.
Six-month moratorium on data center projects. Lifted in late February 2026 after county adopted new regulations. County now expects a potential $15B data center proposal.

Updated land use code to allow data centers with new requirements. Permitted via admin review in industrial zones; requires special review in agricultural areas. Restrictions on noise, power, and water usage.

Planning Commission approved the Project Taurus data center 6-2 with restrictions including a 50 MW limit and utility data publication requirements. An appeal was filed; City Council decision expected in September 2026.

Trustees voted 4-2 on August 31, 2026 to impose a 12-month moratorium on data center applications while staff study infrastructure demands, water use and setbacks; it can end early if regulations are completed sooner.
Commissioners postponed a vote on a proposed 6-to-12-month data center moratorium to October 13, 2026 to gather public input; the planning commission recommends a 6-month maximum if adopted.
The City Council scheduled a vote for November 2, 2026 on an indefinite moratorium on new data centers, which requires seven votes to pass; it would not affect the already-approved Trident project.
Planning and Zoning Commission banned data centers larger than 12,500 sq ft after a year-long moratorium, blocking NE Edge's proposed 1.5M sq ft campus.

The zoning commission opened discussions on a possible moratorium covering data centers, battery storage and solar, despite having no relevant zoning rules in place and no formal applications received. Discussion was set to continue at the commission's August meeting.

The Planning and Zoning Commission is weighing a one-year moratorium on new data centers and battery energy storage systems. At its October 26, 2026 meeting it postponed the public hearing to November 23 at the Town Hall Annex so commissioners can review how the restrictions would affect ordinary home and business battery installations.

The Planning and Zoning Commission is reconsidering a six-month moratorium on new data center development after an initial version failed in a vote; a public hearing is set for December 3, 2026. The revival follows disclosure of emails showing town officials discussed a Geer Street project with developer Global Common for over a year.
County Council unanimously approved first-in-state data center zoning regulations: 1,000-foot buffer from residential zones, ban on open-loop cooling, decommissioning fund requirements.
DNREC denied Project Washington data center under the Coastal Zone Act, classifying it as heavy industry due to 516 backup diesel generators. Appeals board unanimously upheld the denial.
Council unanimously rejected an ordinance that would have allowed data centers as a conditional use, citing water, sewer, electrical infrastructure and noise concerns.

City Council unanimously approved an 18-month moratorium on data center construction — the first data center moratorium in Delaware — pausing reviews of large energy-use facilities, including those over 30 MW, while the city develops permanent regulations. No data center application had been filed in Dover.
Commissioners voted 5-0 in early July 2026 for a one-year moratorium on hyperscale data centers (50+ MW) through July 2027; a permanent-ban push was signaled for August.

Commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on new data center applications (4-0, with one commissioner recused). The moratorium exempts rezoning applications tied to an 800-plus-acre project proposed near Roan Street earlier in 2026; the planning commission had recommended a two-year pause covering that project, but the county attorney urged the shorter, exempted version to limit legal exposure. The week of October 26, 2026, a DCIP Group rezoning of about 238 acres for a data center campus (part of roughly 826 acres sought) deadlocked 2-2 before the commission and failed.

City Commission approved a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center applications on first reading; second and final reading set for August 3, 2026. Follows opposition to the "Project Swan" facility. Lakeland owns its utility, Lakeland Electric.
County commissioners unanimously approved a 12-month data center moratorium on September 15, 2026, following neighboring DeSoto County's controversial project approval.

Board of County Commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on the acceptance, processing, review and approval of data center and large-scale data processing facility applications in unincorporated Washington County. Exempts facilities where computer equipment is no more than 5% of gross floor area and demand does not exceed 250 kW.

Commissioners voted 5-1 to reject Project Tango, a $2 billion AI data center, without prejudice over diverging water-demand estimates, and approved a temporary halt on large-scale data center applications that went to public hearing August 27, 2026.
City commissioners voted 3-2 against a proposed AI data center ban, with the majority noting existing zoning already prevents such facilities.

The county's data center moratorium took effect in late October 2026. A previously submitted data center application may still proceed under the prior rules, and two commissioners want a permanent ban discussed at a future meeting.

Village Council voted 4-1 in early September 2026 against a proposed pause on hyperscale data center applications sought by residents concerned about the 'Project Growler' and 'Project Beskar' proposals; the same night the council fired the village manager and removed the village attorney, citing the need for stronger regulatory language.

Ordinance No. 2026-05, approved unanimously in September 2026: moratorium on data centers and large-scale power-intensive facilities in unincorporated areas through September 30, 2027, to study water, electricity, and infrastructure impacts given reliance on the Floridan Aquifer. Telecom, public-safety, and previously approved projects exempt.

Vice Mayor Kelly Martinez Semrad proposed a one-year moratorium on AI data center applications, citing a projected 96-million-gallon-per-day groundwater shortfall by 2045; proposal went to the county commission September 15, 2026.
The county Planning & Zoning Commission approved a 12-month data center moratorium on September 15, 2026, despite no currently proposed projects; final county commission action pending.
Commissioners unanimously advanced an 18-month moratorium on large-scale data centers; final vote set for October 13, 2026.

County Commission unanimously adopted an ordinance on September 22, 2026 explicitly prohibiting data centers throughout unincorporated areas; staff confirmed the facilities were not listed as a permitted or conditional use under existing zoning.

City Commission approved an 18-month moratorium on data centers on a 3-2 vote on September 23, 2026, exempting an approximately 900,000-square-foot facility already proposed after the city attorney warned that including the existing application could invite litigation.

County commissioners approved (5-0 final vote) a 12-month moratorium on September 15, 2026 on large commercial data centers with maximum electric demand of 50 MW or more, lasting until new land-development regulations are adopted if sooner; government facilities, schools, hospitals and telecom infrastructure are exempt, and sub-50 MW facilities can still seek special-use permits.

Voters ratified Edgewater's data center ban on November 3, 2026, approving Charter Amendment 4 with ~77% of the vote and writing into the city charter the permanent ban on data centers, AI data centers and crypto mining that the City Council first enacted unanimously on September 14, 2026.

The County Council gave final approval on October 20, 2026 to a permanent ban on large-scale data centers (over 50 MW peak load) in unincorporated Volusia County, following a unanimous 7-0 first reading on October 6; the county had stopped accepting large-scale applications on August 17, and the ban takes effect upon filing with the Florida Department of State.
County commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on AI data centers at an October 19, 2026 hearing in Trenton.

County commissioners voted unanimously on October 20, 2026 to begin drafting a one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers in unincorporated Broward County; a final vote is expected in November, possibly December.

Commissioners approved on first reading (reported October 19, 2026) a 12-month moratorium halting building permits, site plans, development orders, special exceptions, rezonings and comprehensive plan amendments tied to data centers, citing water concerns; it takes effect only if adopted on second reading.
22-mile Beltline radius requires special use permits for data centers.
Moratorium on data center development, originally adopted December 2025 and extended in July 2026 to run through early 2027. Triggered by a 1M sq ft proposal on 95 acres.
Temporary moratorium on data center construction.
Temporary moratorium on data center construction.
Temporary moratorium on data center construction.
Temporary moratorium on data center construction.
One-year moratorium expired November 2025. County now drafting permanent regulations.
Resolution 2025-193 placing moratorium on new data centers
Moratorium enacted after data center proposal denied; extended March 2026 for 3 more months
Moratorium on new data center applications in unincorporated areas

Board of Commissioners voted May 5, 2026 to adopt a six-month moratorium on new data centers — the first county on Georgia's coast to do so — amid a contested industrial-park rezoning push for a Kingsland-area site (the related 700-acre rezoning was withdrawn May 5).
Commissioners considered extending the county's existing data center moratorium in late May 2026 while finalizing a permanent data center ordinance, framing it as 'protection, not invitation.'
Commission approved a 30-day moratorium on accepting data center applications; an extension to 180 days is pending an August 6, 2026 hearing.
Council adopted a temporary moratorium running through December 31, 2026 and postponed a pending data center rezoning.
Commissioners approved a 30-day moratorium on data center development with plans to extend the pause into early 2027 while zoning rules are drafted.

Board of Commissioners unanimously suspended new data center applications, zoning requests and civil plan reviews until January 1, 2027, to allow officials to overhaul county land-use codes and evaluate safety guidelines for large-scale technology facilities. The vote followed months of resident protest over zoning loopholes.
Augusta commissioners voted to extend the city's existing moratorium on new data centers while officials continue work on permanent regulations.
City adopted a 12-month moratorium on data centers in early August 2026.
First reading of a strict data center ordinance requiring a 1,500-foot buffer, three-mile separation from water bodies and farmland, and a pledge of no tax abatement.

City Council approved a 90-day moratorium in early September 2026 to draft zoning changes defining data center uses, establish residential buffers and create a community advisory committee; the city previously allowed data centers by right and Digital Realty has already built a facility there.

Commissioners voted unanimously on August 31, 2026 to extend the county data center moratorium another 180 days, with no cap on renewals, while ordinances addressing noise, setbacks and water use are drafted.

Commissioners voted 4-3 to reject a proposed text amendment that would have permanently banned data centers, but kept the county's existing moratorium in place through December 31, 2026 for continued study.

City Council approved an ordinance on September 29, 2026 banning data center construction citywide, repealing the special administrative permit article that would have allowed them. The ban followed opposition to Stillwater Development's proposed 3.5-million-square-foot campus near schools.

City commission approved on first reading (4-2) on September 30, 2026 an ordinance defining data centers and permitting them only as a conditional use in light industrial zones; a second reading was scheduled for October 6. Residents urged a complete moratorium instead.

Commissioners voted unanimously on October 13, 2026 to extend the county’s moratorium on land-use applications to January 14, 2027 — the second extension of a pause that began April 14, 2026. No applications have been received.

The County Commission passed a technology zoning ordinance covering data centers at its late-October 2026 meeting. No land is currently zoned for the new district, so any project requires a full rezoning with multiple public meetings.
Commissioners approved a 182-day moratorium on data center building permits citing aquifer protection. Later replaced with permanent regulations banning data centers over the aquifer.
Developing Data Center Zoning Ordinance Amendment to regulate data centers and protect neighboring property owners and the environment.
Enacted 6-month moratorium on new data center construction to study energy and water impacts.
Proposed moratorium on data center construction in Chicago suburb. Under city council review.

County Board approved 12-month moratorium (April 23, 2026) on data centers with 10,000+ sq ft processing areas in unincorporated areas. Over 100 residents attended to support the measure. Initial 9-month proposal extended to 12 months after staff indicated insufficient capacity for shorter timeline. County data center task force created in February 2026 to develop permanent zoning standards.

Town Council voted 6-1 on September 21, 2026 to extend the moratorium (originally a six-month pause adopted May 2026) through May 31, 2027, halting applications, processing, approvals and permits for data centers while officials await possible state legislation (the 'Power Act') and coordinate with neighboring Bloomington.
City Council voted unanimously for a six-month moratorium on data centers using more than 5 MW, requiring at least two public hearings during the pause.

A moratorium resolution directing a comprehensive regulatory review was referred to the Code and Regulation Committee. Existing annexation agreements would be honored and data centers remain excluded from TIF incentives.

Residents filed suit alleging that improper private discussions over an $18 billion, 472-acre data center campus violated the Open Meetings Act, seeking to void 2024-2025 approvals and halt further permits.

Eight-month moratorium on data center development in unincorporated areas (through May 2027), adopted after more than 1,200 public comments. Grayslake's municipally approved $18 billion T5 campus is exempt.
City Council gave first reading (reported the week of September 21-24, 2026) to a 180-day moratorium ordinance on data centers while awaiting possible state legislation.

City officials determined its zoning code does not currently permit data centers — creating a de facto moratorium — and are evaluating whether to adopt a formal pause while regulations are written, as reported September 30, 2026.

The County Board unanimously approved a nine-month moratorium on data center applications on October 28, 2026, in effect until July 28, 2027 unless the board lifts it sooner. No applications can be filed during the pause while the county writes a data center ordinance; the board's land use committee and the Zoning Board of Appeals each unanimously recommended approval, and the only rule proposed so far would confine data centers to industrial zones.
1-year moratorium. Triggered by 500 MW, 300-acre Decennial Group campus proposal.
12-month moratorium on hyperscale data centers.
Up to 1-year moratorium on data centers, solar, and battery storage.
1-year moratorium, expired February 2026.
Temporary moratorium on data center construction.
1-year moratorium on wind, solar, data centers, and SMRs.
12-month moratorium, unanimous vote. APC recommended 5-0

After the City-County Council's non-binding Proposal 158 urging a pause, the Metropolitan Development Commission voted 5-3 on July 1, 2026 to recommend a new special-use (SU-47) zoning class for high-impact data centers; final City-County Council approval is expected in August 2026.
A proposed moratorium blocking data centers over 100,000 sq ft advanced to a final Council vote scheduled for July 16, 2026.

The City-County Council development committee voted 10-3 on July 13, 2026 to advance a pause on new data center approvals running through the end of 2027, with Mayor Joe Hogsett's support. The measure was scheduled for a full council vote on August 10, 2026. Opponents of the separately approved DC BLOX project at Washington Street and Shadeland Avenue have also discussed litigation.
City Council advanced moratorium Ordinance No. 16, 2026; the Plan Commission takes it up August 4, 2026.
Residents are calling for a temporary moratorium while commissioners draft regulations. The county confirmed it signed a non-disclosure agreement with an unnamed data center developer.

City-County Council voted 23-1 for a binding moratorium barring new data center construction through December 31, 2027; ratified by the Metropolitan Development Commission on August 19, 2026. Three approved projects (DC Blox, Metrobloks, Sabey) are exempt.
First reading of a proposed moratorium on data centers and battery storage facilities running through December 31, 2027. Special meeting for public comment and vote scheduled August 27, 2026.

City Council voted 9-0 on August 27, 2026 for a moratorium on data center and battery storage facility applications running until December 2027, while the city studies electrical capacity, water usage, public safety, traffic, noise and environmental impacts. Applies only to the city, not Elkhart County.

City Council defeated the proposed one-year data center moratorium on a 4-4 tie vote on October 13, 2026. The measure, introduced by Councilwoman Rohli Booker in September, would have paused rezonings, annexations and tax abatements for large data centers (Google's operating campus was exempt). The council also rejected a data center task force resolution 5-3, after Michelle Chambers switched her vote from September 22.

Town Council approved a one-year moratorium on September 21, 2026 covering data centers, solar farms, wind farms and battery storage systems — uses that lack permitted categories in the zoning code — and directed the planning department and Plan Commission to review the code.
County commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on new data center development on September 22, 2026, temporarily blocking projects while the county works on permanent regulations.

A permanent Data Center Overlay district is advancing (reported October 22, 2026), requiring site-specific rezoning votes, a 55 dB noise cap at homes, 300-foot building and 500-foot equipment setbacks, a once-through cooling ban, peak-day water caps, and decommissioning assurances; public hearings are set for November 2 and 9. The driver is Alcoa's ~700-acre Project Alloy.
Temporary moratorium on construction of data centers in unincorporated areas due to absence of county zoning ordinances pertaining to data centers.
One-year moratorium on rezoning, site plans, and building permits for data centers in unincorporated areas. Concerns about water pollution, power usage, and facility siting.

One of the nation's strictest local data center zoning ordinances. Requires comprehensive water studies, 1,000-foot residential setbacks, noise and light limits, and community betterment fund contributions.
Indefinite moratorium. Triggered by 200 MW Applied Digital proposal.
Commissioners approved moratorium while creating an ordinance
Supervisors passed a 12-month moratorium on data centers at a special meeting on May 26, 2026.

In its third consecutive meeting on the subject, the City Council voted 5-2 on July 28, 2026 to schedule an August 10 public hearing on a four-month data center moratorium; Councilors Jeff Schneider and Greg Nichols opposed. The city administrator said she would recommend suspending the additional-reading requirement so the council could take final action on the ordinance at that same August 10 meeting. Marshalltown has no data center-specific regulations and no project has been formally proposed.

City ended preliminary discussions with developer Gronen over a South Highway 61 Industrial Park facility and said it will review Heavy Industrial District regulations governing future data center development. No nondisclosure agreements were signed.

City Council rejected a proposed one-year data center moratorium 3-2 on August 21, 2026, after Google was identified as the developer behind a local project; one council member switched position on learning the developer’s identity.

Board of Supervisors unanimously approved (6-0) a six-month, extendable moratorium on September 23, 2026 covering data centers, AI computing, data mining and cryptocurrency operations, while the county develops regulations 'from scratch' with monthly work sessions.

A county data center zoning ordinance to replace the existing moratorium advanced 4-1 at second reading (reported week of October 19, 2026); the final reading is set for October 27, and the moratorium lifts when the ordinance is published.
Board of supervisors passed Resolution 2027-11 on a 2-1 vote on September 28, 2026, imposing a 12-month moratorium on data center development in effect until permanent zoning is adopted.
90-day moratorium on data center permits, extended to June 11, 2026. Two data center developers seeking 1,000+ acres in western Sedgwick County.
County Commission considering a moratorium lasting one to two years while developing regulations. Prompted by Osawatomie's $1B data center proposal.
~3 year moratorium on data centers in unincorporated areas.
City Commission unanimously approved a two-year moratorium on large-scale data centers, extending an originally proposed one-year pause, while staff study longer-term code changes.

County Commission approved a six-month moratorium on data centers and battery energy storage systems, in effect until January 22, 2027, plus a separate commercial solar moratorium expiring December 1, 2026.

City Commission approved three ordinances establishing a digital infrastructure district and associated zoning protections. A citizen petition seeking an outright data center prohibition was not acted upon and could advance to the November 2026 ballot.
Temporary moratorium on the planning, establishment, and construction of data centers in the county, adopted September 2, 2026 and running until December 31, 2028.

The City Council unanimously adopted a 12-month moratorium (reported mid-September 2026) defining data centers broadly — hyperscale, cloud, AI and cryptocurrency facilities — while the Planning Commission reviews zoning code amendments.

County commissioners unanimously delayed action on October 6, 2026 on proposed data center regulations covering siting, noise, lighting, water and decommissioning — previously approved by the zoning board — and will revisit them on October 27.

The city is drafting data center rules with noise caps of 60 dB daytime and 50 dB nighttime at the property line (reported the week of October 26, 2026). A planning commission hearing is set for November 10, with council consideration expected December 1.
Citizen initiative banning high-impact data centers and large battery storage facilities approved with 71.5% of the vote (2,966-1,183, unofficial) on November 3, 2026.

Citizen-initiated ban on high-impact data center facilities approved with ~60% of the vote on November 3, 2026. The measure reached the ballot by court order and a validation lawsuit remains pending; it sits in tension with the city's July 2026 digital infrastructure district ordinances.
Voter-approved ban on data centers above 25 MW passed with ~72% of the vote on November 3, 2026.
Fiscal Court voted 4-2 to pass a 150-day moratorium on data center applications. Extended indefinitely until new regulations are approved. Triggered by a $6B, 600MW proposal that was later withdrawn.

Fiscal Court approved a six-month moratorium on data center applications as a proactive measure, despite no expressed developer interest. In late September 2026 the Fiscal Court extended the moratorium.
Fiscal Court adopted countywide moratorium on new data center and large-scale IT infrastructure facility applications. Also rejected a rezoning proposal for a 138-acre data center site.
Fiscal Court restricted data storage centers to Heavy Industrial (I-2) zones only, requiring conditional use permits. Developer TenKey LandCo sued to overturn the ordinance.
Councilmember filed ordinance proposing a 6-month moratorium on data center approvals. Tabled indefinitely and expired without action in March 2026.
180-day moratorium passed by Board of Commissioners

A one-year moratorium on data centers took effect in August 2026 after the Fiscal Court's July 29 first reading and August second reading. On September 28, 2026 the Fiscal Court unanimously rejected proposed zoning regulations that would have created an 'industrial technology' district for hyperscale data centers near the E.W. Brown Generating Station, sending the regulations back to the planning commission; the moratorium remains in effect.

A standing-room-only public forum on July 29, 2026 drew near-unanimous resident opposition, with essentially every hand in the room raised against future data centers. Judge-Executive Jason Marshall said he would ask the fiscal court for a long-term moratorium to allow the county time to study infrastructure, farmland, utility and emergency-service impacts; the vote was scheduled for August 11, 2026. There are no current data center proposals or agreements in the county.

Fiscal Court unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on new data centers and data storage facilities at a special meeting on July 9, 2026, without discussion. The ordinance exempts the EastPark Industrial Park, leaving TeraWulf's planned Muskie Data Campus unaffected.

Metro Council voted 24-1 for a six-month moratorium barring planners from approving new data center proposals until the council adopts comprehensive zoning rules. Advanced 7-1 out of the Planning and Zoning Committee on August 4, 2026.
City passed a six-month moratorium on data centers as residents sought time to understand impacts on electric bills, property taxes and water.

Fiscal Court approved a two-year moratorium on large-scale data centers in early September 2026; the county has no zoning regulations and plans to consider a conditional-use review process during the pause. No projects have been proposed.

The fiscal court unanimously approved a permanent ban on data center construction (reported September 14, 2026), alongside restrictions on landfills and battery storage — described as the first Kentucky county to permanently ban data centers.

City Council voted unanimously on September 30, 2026 to direct legal counsel to draft an ordinance banning 'mega' hyperscale data center facilities (excluding smaller operations); the ban requires Planning & Zoning Commission approval before taking effect. Neighboring Scott County extended its own moratorium the prior week. The week of October 26, 2026 the council unanimously approved a second extension of the city's data center moratorium, through June 30, 2027, while the citywide ban on hyperscale data centers is drafted.

Urban County Council passed its pause on data center permits, development plans and zone changes on June 9, 2026, and on October 8, 2026 voted to extend the moratorium through October 2027. The debate followed DartPoints' purchase of an 81,000-square-foot property off New Circle Road described as drawing up to 70 MW.
The Fiscal Court approved 4-1 a one-year moratorium on new data centers and expansions on October 21, 2026, with exceptions possible.
City Council voted 6-0 to impose a one-year ban on data center construction, expansion, or establishment citywide. Could last up to 2 years.

A commissioner proposed a two-year moratorium on tax incentives for data centers; referred to the special projects committee. The parish attorney noted state law requires a master plan before a moratorium can be adopted.
The Parish Council approved a 90-day moratorium on data center development without objection on October 26, 2026; the item returns to the council on January 21, 2027.

City Council enacted a six-month moratorium banning data centers to give the city time to adjust its Land Development Code. Originally fast-tracked after sudden industry pressure; enacted approximately April 21, 2026.

Halted a proposed data center amid public outcry over safety and water/resource use concerns.

Town Council voted unanimously on November 4, 2026 to prohibit data centers in all zoning districts, then lifted the 180-day emergency moratorium adopted in June. Town Council unanimously enacted a 180-day data center moratorium in early June 2026, alongside Scarborough.
Voters approved a 180-day data center moratorium (extendable) at a special town meeting on July 8, 2026.
Planning Board unanimously recommended a permanent ban on data centers across all zoning districts; the recommendation goes to the city council for adoption.
Town councilors voted unanimously to send a proposed permanent data center ban to the planning board for public hearing, building on the temporary moratorium enacted in June 2026.
City Council unanimously enacted a six-month moratorium on data centers in industrial zones on October 5, 2026, retroactive to September 8; it expires in March 2027 and can be extended to June.

Board of County Commissioners approved a 12-month moratorium on data center applications in unincorporated areas on June 30, 2026. On September 30, 2026 the county announced a multi-year regulatory timeline, with a public hearing on permanent regulations planned for June 2027.

County Council voted 7-0 on October 5, 2026 to enact an amended Bill 63-26 imposing a moratorium on new data centers through January 31, 2028 — or until comprehensive data center legislation is adopted — replacing an earlier proposal for an outright ban.

City Council unanimously approved a zoning amendment on October 6, 2026 setting a 200-foot setback for data processing centers from existing or planned trails, matching the setback from homes; the council also supports further review, possibly including a size-based framework, alongside the land development code update.

Permanent zoning regulations requiring any cryptocurrency mining or data center operation to purchase or develop enough new renewable energy to offset 100% of its electrical consumption.
County commissioners approved an interim zoning moratorium of up to one year on new data centers while permanent regulations are drafted.

County clerk accepted 3,652 signatures for a data center ballot initiative on July 31, 2026 but rejected the initiative on August 10. A district court judge is weighing the challenge, with a decision expected in late August.

County Planning & Zoning Commission unanimously recommended an 18-month moratorium on data centers on June 16, 2026; awaiting a Board of Supervisors final vote. In early September 2026 commissioners held a public hearing, drawing roughly 30 speakers, on a request to extend the county pause from 8 to 18 months, with a decision expected within two weeks.
City adopted a six-month moratorium on data centers, extendable by up to 12 additional months.

First NJ municipality to ban data centers. Passed Ordinance 10-2026 prohibiting the construction and operation of data centers.
Township Council introduced ordinance to eliminate data centers from the Hexa Builders Redevelopment Plan, reversing a June 2025 zoning change.

A measure to ban data centers outright is on Hubbard's November 2026 ballot — the only full ban among the Ohio communities with data center measures before voters.
Issue 10 — ban on data centers above 25 MW approved with ~65% of the vote on November 3, 2026.
Voter-approved ban on data centers above 25 MW passed with ~65% on November 3, 2026.
Voter-approved data center ban passed with ~82% on November 3, 2026.

Issue 28 approved with ~55% on November 3, 2026 — requires citywide voter approval for developments over 50 acres, 20 MW of power, or 500,000 gallons of water per day, and adds community-impact standards.
Citywide data center ban approved with ~77% of the vote on November 3, 2026 (separate from Hubbard Township's existing moratorium).
Voters adopted county zoning for unincorporated areas on November 3, 2026 (~60% yes), so data center construction requires compatible zoning.
Voters adopted county zoning for unincorporated areas on November 3, 2026 (~53% yes), so data center construction requires compatible zoning.
Issue 25 approved with ~61% on November 3, 2026, capping data centers at 25 MW. The measure grew out of a signature drive prompted by a Vantage Data Centers project near Wynn and Corduroy roads.
Voter-approved ban on large data center facilities passed with ~74% on November 3, 2026, following the council's August rejection of Aligned Data Centers' 200 MW site plan.

Issue 16 approved with ~87% (946-140 unofficial) on November 3, 2026 — requires financial guarantees from hyperscale data centers seeking tax abatements, PILOT programs or special tax designations, amending Chapter 133.01 of the village code.
Charter amendment banning data centers approved with ~77% of the vote on November 3, 2026.
Citywide data center ban approved with ~77% of the vote on November 3, 2026, amid the city's ongoing zoning litigation with Thor Equities.

Voters overturned four rezonings (covering roughly 550 acres, including SR 730 and McGuinn Road parcels) that would have allowed data center construction, each referendum failing with ~80% opposed, on November 3, 2026.
City Council unanimously approved a nine-month moratorium on new data center construction through December 31, 2026. Exempts existing projects.
Google data center rezoning triggered recall effort against entire City Council and a lawsuit challenging the land deal. 1,600+ signatures gathered.
City leaders approved a data center moratorium lasting through end of 2026.

Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Jr. banned hyperscale data centers on tribally owned and trust lands after a task force survey found 64% of nearly 1,600 tribal citizens opposed. Projects on non-tribal land within the reservation now require tribal government consultation.

Residents are gathering signatures on three citizen initiative petitions regarding the 'Project Open Sky' data center — a temporary moratorium, noise standards, and a voter-approval requirement — each needing 172 valid signatures for ballot placement.
Legislation (ONCA 26-70) introduced in the Osage Nation Congress on September 30, 2026 would require tribal Congress approval before hyperscale data center projects can proceed on Osage Nation lands.

Tribal citizens voted 261-83 (with 7 abstentions) at the tribes' annual Tribal Council meeting in early October 2026 to impose a three-year moratorium on data center construction on tribal lands, running through October 2029, citing water use, environmental effects and transparency concerns. Gov. Reggie Wassana said no data center agreement has been signed. (Tribal headquarters are in Concho, Canadian County; tribal jurisdiction spans multiple western Oklahoma counties.)
Enterprise zone tax break moratorium affecting data center development in the region where Google operates large facilities.

City Council unanimously adopted a 120-day land use moratorium on new and expanded data centers on July 27, 2026; it remains in effect until November 24, 2026 while the city finalizes permanent zoning restrictions.

The City Council unanimously approved a 120-day moratorium (reported September 16, 2026) halting acceptance, review and approval of data storage/processing facility proposals while the city evaluates water, energy and infrastructure needs.

City Council gave final approval on September 22, 2026 to a 120-day moratorium (expiring January 19, 2027) and established a Data Center Task Force to study regulations, with public town halls October 6 and 20 and recommendations due to the council in December.

City Council advanced permanent data center restrictions on October 6, 2026, limiting primary-use data centers mainly to Industrial Park and Industrial Sanctuary zones capped at 608 acres (down from roughly 6,600 acres eligible today), requiring public hearings, capping accessory data centers, and adding a temporary 1,000-foot school buffer; second reading and possible final vote set for October 20.
County commissioners unanimously approved a 120-day temporary moratorium on data centers in unincorporated Clackamas County on October 22, 2026, effective immediately.

Township approved amendments eliminating a six-parcel data center overlay district; data centers are now conditional uses in industrial zones, which officials said strengthens resident protections while preserving local oversight.
Township adopted a 20-page data center ordinance covering setbacks, lighting, noise limits, environmental impacts and electricity use.
Township supervisors unanimously advanced a draft zoning ordinance that would allow data centers only as conditional uses in light-industrial districts, with adoption possible in October 2026.

Supervisors approved Ordinance 6-26 regulating data centers, limiting facility size and proximity to residential and agricultural areas; the planning commission is reviewing further amendments on noise and water-use standards.

Temporary ban on new data center and power-plant applications proposed after Nadara's interest in 800 acres near Gans; ordinance votes postponed to September 17, 2026 to meet state notice requirements. Proposed rules include 200-foot property-line setbacks and noise limits.

The Planning Commission is considering a zoning amendment (reviewed September 23, 2026) limiting data centers to Heavy Manufacturing and Manufacturing Commercial districts through a conditional use process, with a 500-foot setback from Preservation districts (1,000 feet for major facilities); a vote is possible at the October 20 workshop. The city's existing 180-day application moratorium expires January 2027.
The Planning Commission reviewed a draft curative amendment on data centers (reported the week of September 21-24, 2026); a public comment period is opening, with hearings possibly in mid-November.

Township ordinance restricting data centers to the industrial zoning district — large-scale projects would need a special exception and smaller projects planning commission review. A public hearing was scheduled for October 12, 2026, with possible final approval the same night.

City Council gave 7-0 initial approval on October 6, 2026 to the city's first data center zoning rules, requiring a public hearing, water/power/noise/heat impact studies and a 1,000-foot buffer from homes and schools; final vote set for October 20. A previously filed Route 22 project at 2184 Industrial Drive is exempt and goes before the Planning Commission November 12.

The county Planning Commission on October 8, 2026 weighed a revised data center zoning amendment that would cut largest-facility setbacks from 2,000 to 1,250 feet and loosen noise limits versus the May draft; the amendment, which would apply in 19 municipalities relying on county zoning, must clear the commission before going to County Council. In late October 2026, County Council began discussing an ordinance for the 19 municipalities under county zoning that would require a special exception from the Zoning Hearing Board for every data center; a second work session is pending.

The public hearing on the township’s data center ordinance closed October 14, 2026; council could adopt it November 4. Data centers would be a conditional use only in the L-I district on lots of at least 12 acres, with buildings capped at 35 feet (45 feet with an extra 50-foot setback), power only from a regional electric utility, and diesel generators limited to backup use.

County commissioners unanimously approved a data center ordinance on October 20, 2026 requiring a 1,000-foot setback from homes, noise limits, outdoor lighting limits, and a pre-application public meeting.

Supervisors unanimously approved Ordinance #10-14-26 regulating data centers (reported October 19, 2026), requiring a decommissioning plan and a community benefits agreement, though with looser setbacks and noise limits than the planning commission had requested.

Town Council voted 4-1 on May 5, 2026 to adopt a zoning ordinance banning data centers in all districts for roughly two years, one day after Hanton City Investments filed its application for a several-hundred-acre woodland site.

Town Council voted 5-0 to prohibit data centers and battery energy storage systems, citing reliance on well water and septic systems and contamination risk. Second Rhode Island town to ban data centers.
A proposed zoning ordinance restricting data centers was referred to a town council subcommittee, with a public hearing to follow review.
County Council approved a one-year moratorium 4-3 and separately barred data centers from industrial districts.

County Council voted 5-1 on third and final reading on September 21, 2026 to approve a one-year freeze on new data centers, with amendments exempting facilities of 65 MW or less that locate in an established industrial park or on a former industrial site, do not self-generate power (except emergency backup), and are used primarily for data storage/processing. After adjourning, council reconvened to 'reconsider' the vote — a press association attorney said the unposted meeting was illegal and the reconsideration vote not in effect.
Council Chair Bernie Hamby directed staff to draft a temporary moratorium; the proposal is expected on the August 18, 2026 County Council agenda.

County Council delayed the final vote from August to September 21, 2026, when it passed the 12-month moratorium 5-1 with size- and site-based carveouts. The $2.8 billion NorthMark project already under construction is unaffected.

County Council's temporary moratorium on data centers, cryptocurrency mining and data-processing facilities in unincorporated areas — pausing applications, permits, rezoning and incentives — passed second reading on September 28, 2026; a third and final reading is still required. The ordinance would close a zoning gap that allows facilities by right in unincorporated areas.

Officials set a debate on a 120-day moratorium on data center proposals aimed at closing loopholes that allow hyperscale facilities in light industrial zones; the mayor said such centers 'will not be permitted.'
County Council unanimously approved a data center moratorium on third and final reading on September 15, 2026, closing permitting loopholes while it studies environmental and community impacts.

County Council unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data centers, cryptocurrency mining and data processing facilities on third and final reading on September 23, 2026, to provide time to develop regulations.
County released a timeline on September 29, 2026 for adopting a 12-month data center moratorium, including three town halls and a public hearing planned for March 2027.
County Council unanimously confirmed a 12-month moratorium on accepting new data center permits at third reading on July 15, 2026 (first passed June 2026); the council may extend it.

City Council gave second and final approval on November 2, 2026 to a 150-day moratorium on data center development within city limits, running through late March 2027, while council and staff assess utility, environmental and land-use impacts and consider new zoning standards. Newberry County separately has a 12-month moratorium.
~15 month moratorium on data centers and crypto mines. Vote: 13-2.
City enacted an 18-month moratorium on June 3, 2026 covering data centers, Bitcoin mining, and microchip manufacturing.
Commission adopted a one-year moratorium on data centers, applying to rural and unincorporated areas only.

City Commission unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on land use applications and building permits for new data centers and bitcoin mines in the I-2 heavy industrial district, paired with a text amendment limiting data centers to I-2. On May 21, 2026 the Commission unanimously extended the pause from June 5 to December 3, 2026 to study noise impacts.

Commission voted 16-0 to limit data centers to the M-2 Special Impact Industrial District, closing a loophole that had allowed them in agricultural zoning. Additional conditional use standards are still being developed.
City enacted an 18-month moratorium on data centers and cryptocurrency mining, blocking permits despite no current projects proposed.

12-month moratorium advanced unanimously by City Council after a 5-2 Planning Commission recommendation, with a formal vote set for the week of September 14, 2026; paired zoning ordinance adds noise/odor reviews, utility assessments, and 200- to 500-foot setbacks. A response to Meta's existing campus.

On October 20, 2026 the City Council rejected an 18-month data center moratorium on a 6-6 tie, then passed 7-5 a substitute (Ordinance 18 as amended) imposing a 135-day pause on data center construction and applications while siting and operating rules are written. A federal judge had reversed the council's bans barring six protesters from chambers ahead of the vote.

City Council is advancing initial zoning rules limiting data centers to heavy industrial districts with 500-foot setbacks from homes, schools and government buildings and requiring equipment indoors; a second reading is next, with further regulations expected in about three months.

The Board of Mayor and Aldermen approved Resolution 44-2026 on October 12, 2026 — a six-month moratorium on development applications for non-grid power generation, accessory computing and industrial-scale computing facilities. It took effect immediately and expires April 12, 2027 unless extended; applications already accepted are exempt.
A proposed moratorium on data centers in unincorporated Shelby County passed first reading 5-4 on October 12, 2026.
The Regional Planning Commission voted unanimously on October 12, 2026 to recommend a 12-month moratorium on new data center development; the recommendation now goes to county officials.
The Board passed on first reading, 4-2, an ordinance that would allow data centers only in the industrial district, where they are currently unrestricted; final action is expected in November 2026.

County commissioners voted 17-4 on October 19, 2026 to approve tight limits on future data centers: residential setbacks raised from 100 to 500 feet, sites limited to 10-100 acres, noise caps, and requirements that applicants prove water and power capacity and pay for utility upgrades; further zoning action returns in November.
City Council voted 5-2 to deny a land use map change for CloudBurst Data Centers. Concerns centered on water use (up to 70,000 gallons/day) during drought conditions on the Edwards Aquifer.
City Council approved a 120-day moratorium (one dissent) around May 20, 2026 to study infrastructure and water impacts.

Commissioners approved a roughly one-year pause (3-2) on May 12, 2026 on large battery, power, and data center projects in unincorporated areas; a developer filed suit on May 28 arguing the moratorium is illegal under Texas law.

City Council voted 4-3 to define data centers in the zoning code and make them ineligible in all districts — the first citywide data center ban in Texas, adopted under home-rule authority. A state preemption challenge is expected.

City adopted a Data Center Policy Framework requiring a Special Permit with public hearings, stricter environmental standards for water, energy, wastewater, noise, lighting and ecology, elimination of local economic incentives for hyperscale projects, and encouragement of Community Benefit Agreements.

City Council voted unanimously to take the first step toward a 90-day moratorium on data center construction, alongside a three-part regulatory plan creating an 11-member Data Center and Infrastructure Commission. Commission findings due November 3, 2026; final council vote scheduled February 16, 2027.

City Council voted unanimously to pursue litigation against neighboring Westlake over a proposed 1.1 million-square-foot data center sited 506 feet from Keller homes, and simultaneously initiated a 90-day moratorium process (expanded from an initial 30-day proposal).

County commissioners approved a resolution requesting state-level protections and a pause on data center development, citing water use, electricity costs, and infrastructure impacts, and asking the Legislature for expanded county regulatory authority.

County rescinded its May 12, 2026 one-year moratorium in June 2026 after a developer sued for more than $100 million in damages, replacing it with developer requirements. Tom Green County subsequently abandoned its own planned moratorium.

Petition-led 18-month moratorium heading to a City Council vote in late September 2026. In the week of September 7-10, 2026 the council unanimously passed a nonbinding resolution pledging to hold off on large-scale data centers until rules on water, electricity, setbacks, screening, and lighting are drafted.

City staff proposed ordinance options that would allow stand-alone data centers only in light industrial and industrial manufacturing districts with a specific use permit, or in planned development districts when specifically identified — with a 300-foot residential setback, a 75-foot height limit, no evaporative cooling, and daytime and nighttime noise limits with testing before and after construction. Staff describe the rules as a work in progress.
Commission approved a 180-day pause on new data center and related power-plant applications on May 26, 2026. The Pronghorn project is exempt; the Red Butte project is paused.
City Council unanimously voted to deny a rezoning application for a 66,000 sq ft data center, citing need to complete economic master plan first.
Voters approved a five-year moratorium on AI and crypto data center construction at Town Meeting Day by show of hands.
Permanent ban on data centers enacted 6-0. Blocked Amazon's 220,000 sq ft proposal on 42 acres.
Partial restrictions on 22M sq ft Digital Gateway project (Compass, QTS, Amazon). Vote: 6-0.

Supervisors deferred to November 17, 2026 a vote on a 12-month 'Legislative Pause on Data Center and Substation Applications,' retroactive to September 15, 2026 and covering 33 active applications, after staff requested more time; the county attorney advised a full moratorium would not be legal under Virginia law.

City Council unanimously approved a zoning ordinance limiting data centers to conditional uses in industrial zones, prohibiting groundwater use, closing by-right development loopholes and removing the Fentress Overlay district exception. An eight-month application pause remains in effect.

Supervisors voted 6-1 to direct staff to draft a temporary moratorium on new data center applications; a vote is scheduled for September 15, 2026. Amazon has filed a by-right site plan for four buildings on the former GWU campus to bypass planning commission review.

Board of Supervisors adopted a new Data Center District ordinance on August 25, 2026 requiring rezoning plus a special use permit, 1,000-foot setbacks from non-industrial properties, a 50 dBA noise limit, closed-loop cooling only, and mandatory water-use studies.
Town Council voted 6-0 in September 2026 to require conditional use permits for all data centers, eliminating by-right status in industrial zones to ensure public input.

The Board of Supervisors voted 8-0 on September 22, 2026 to end by-right data center development countywide: facilities outside designated opportunity zones now require Special Use Permits with public hearings, and the Data Center Opportunity Zone Overlay District shrinks from about 9,700 acres to roughly 3,641 acres.

The Planning Commission voted 8-0 in mid-September 2026 to recommend prohibiting data centers as a primary use in every city zoning district — blocking new standalone data center projects outright, while exempting network hubs within offices, hospitals and similar uses. City Council votes on the recommendation October 21, 2026.
City Council passed an emergency ~1-year moratorium (9-0) on June 9, 2026 on new large data centers (over 20 MVA), extendable by six months, paired with a policy-study resolution.
City Council passed an emergency one-year citywide data center moratorium (6-1, Ordinance C36887) on June 23, 2026.

County proposed a nine-month building permit moratorium on data centers in unincorporated areas, expiring after the 2027 legislative session, after the utility paused permit processing. Triggers a staff review of infrastructure, water, energy and zoning and would add data center definitions to county code.

Town Council enacted a temporary moratorium on accepting data center permit applications lasting at least six months, despite having received no applications or inquiries. Staff will draft an ordinance addressing data centers using Skagit County's definition; the county adopted a similar moratorium for unincorporated areas on June 1, 2026. A public hearing is set for August 25, 2026.
Commissioners unanimously approved a four-month moratorium on new data center permits (reduced from a nine-month proposal) to allow staff to develop zoning regulations. Extension possible.
Commissioners unanimously directed staff to draft a six-month data center moratorium following resident concerns about water scarcity, despite no existing applications.

City Council voted 5-1 in early September 2026 to direct staff to draft a six-month moratorium on new data center applications while examining impacts on electric rates, water use, industrial land, noise and the environment, with input from the Planning Commission and Utility Advisory Committee.
The county held the required public hearing on October 5, 2026 for its previously enacted six-month emergency moratorium pausing permits for data centers and battery energy storage systems.
City Council voted on November 3, 2026 to restrict data centers to Mixed-Use Light Industrial zones; a proposed six-month moratorium failed, receiving three of the five votes needed.
County Board voted 29-2 in early June 2026 for an 18-month moratorium on new data centers, prompted by a $1B Meta campus proposed north of Beaver Dam.
Passed the nation's first anti-data center referendum, banning data center construction by public vote.

City moratorium on data center construction. On September 30, 2026 the city unveiled a draft zoning framework that would allow data centers only in designated areas, cap building size at 100,000 square feet (excluding hyperscale campuses) and require 1,000-foot separation between medium and large facilities; council introduction is expected in November with a vote anticipated in January 2027.

County Board voted unanimously on April 28, 2026 for an 18-month moratorium (amended up from one year), with a carve-out allowing one facility of up to 1 petabyte. On September 30, 2026 the county's Planning and Park Commission finalized a 24-page draft permanent ordinance capping developments at under 500 acres with at most 100 acres of agricultural land conversion, defining data centers as 50,000+ square feet on 10+ contiguous acres with 1,000+ servers; a County Board hearing and vote are pending.
Township moratorium on data center construction in the Driftless Area.
Township moratorium on data center development in the Driftless Area.
Common Council passed a moratorium on issuing zoning and building permits for data centers larger than 10,000 square feet.

The Planning and Zoning Committee voted July 29, 2026 to recommend a 12-month data center moratorium after an overflow crowd forced officials to relocate the public meeting to the Woodman's Sports and Convention Center. The ordinance was set to go before the full Town Board on August 3, 2026. No data center has been formally proposed, but the town received an April inquiry describing a concept at North Polzin and West Fenrick roads.
Plan Commission advanced an 18-month data center moratorium on August 3, 2026; public hearing held August 5 and Common Council vote held August 13.
Village board voted unanimously for a one-year moratorium, extendable by six additional months, joining nearby Wrightstown and Manitowoc County.

The Common Council voted unanimously (among members present) on October 13, 2026 for a one-year moratorium on new data center development and expansions while the city writes permanent zoning rules; it ends early if the rules are adopted sooner. Proposed rules would ban facilities over 60,000 square feet, allow those under 20,000 square feet in industrial-heavy zones, and require Board of Zoning Appeals approval for sizes in between.

The city enacted a one-year moratorium on data centers (extendable to 18 months) on October 9, 2026, and on October 20 the council rejected 7-0 a conditional use permit for PNK Group's proposed hyperscale data center.

Voters approved a referendum with ~63% support on November 3, 2026 requiring citywide voter approval before the city commits to the proposed GM/JATCO data center site if the project's cost exceeds $450 million.
City Council defeated a proposed 12-month data center moratorium 8-1 in late May 2026.

As part of the county's first land-use overhaul in more than a decade, commissioners proposed prohibiting data centers outright in most zones and allowing them only by special-use permit in General Rural 20- and 35-acre zones and industrial zones, with public hearings required before both the Planning and Zoning Commission and the commissioners. No data center project has been proposed in the county; commissioners cited overwhelming public opposition and limited information. Industrial zoning is concentrated near Cody and Powell.

City Council annexed and zoned a 34.46-acre parcel as a staging area for North Range Business Park data center construction, over resident objections regarding aquifers, noise and incremental annexation.
